title: Scam Texts and Calls
about: Spot the signs of a scam text or call before you reply.

cards.title: Scams in your pocket
cards.body:
The same tricks as [[phishing]] emails come by **text** and **phone call**. Scam texts often ask for a **small fee**, set a **deadline** and add an **unfamiliar link**.

Callers may say they're your bank or even the police. Hang up if they ask for a **sign-in code**, a **password**, **gift cards** or **secrecy**, or to **control your computer**.

cards.prompt: Your phone rings. It sounds exactly like your cousin. (Computers can now make a [[voice clone|voice-clone]] from a short clip.)

steps.text: **"It's me! I'm in trouble and need $200 in gift cards right now. Don't tell anyone!"** What do you do?

choices.text: Buy the gift cards. It's their voice
choices.consequence: Voices can be copied, and gift cards are a favourite scam payment. The money would be gone.

choices.text: Keep it secret, like they asked
choices.consequence: Secrecy is a warning sign. It stops anyone helping you check.

choices.text: Hang up and call your cousin on their saved number
choices.consequence: Your cousin answers, confused, and fine. It was a scam, and you stopped it.

steps.text: Some families agree a secret **family safe word** for emergencies. What's the best way to check a call like that next time?

choices.text: Ask the caller to say your birthday to prove who they are
choices.consequence: Birthdays are often online, so a scammer may know yours.

choices.text: Listen closely: a copied voice always sounds a bit robotic
choices.consequence: Copied voices can sound just like the real person. Your ears can't be sure.

choices.text: Agree a family safe word that's never posted anywhere
choices.consequence: Now anyone in your family can ask for it. A copied voice won't know it.

cards.explanation: A familiar voice can be faked: **hang up and call back** on a number you know, and agree a **family safe word**. Secrecy and gift cards are warning signs.
cards.hint: How can you reach your cousin in a way a scammer can't fake? And what could only your family know?

items.label: Caller asks for the code texted to you
Caller wants to control your computer
"Pay in gift cards or be arrested"
Caller says to keep it from your family
You call the number on the bank's site
You call a friend on their saved number

cards.explanation: Codes, controlling your computer, gift cards and secrecy are scam signs: **hang up**. Calling a number you found yourself is fine.
cards.hint: Check each against the warning signs for calls, and ask who chose the number.
cards.nudge: Look at each one again: does it match a warning sign, and who chose the number?

cards.prompt: You're expecting a parcel, then this arrives. Tap the **three** scam-text signs in the **new** message.
cards.explanation: It asks for a **small fee**, sets a **deadline** and links to `parcels-redelivery.example`. The sender name can be faked, so it blends in: check in the company's **official app** instead.
cards.hint: In the new message, find what it wants you to pay, how long it gives you, and where it sends you.
cards.nudge: Look for a fee, a deadline and a link in the new message, one at a time.

cards.prompt: Some scams are **too good to be true**: free coins, a prize, an easy job paying lots. Which is **always** a warning sign?

options.text: Being asked to pay a fee in gift cards to claim a prize
A text from a number that isn't saved in your phone
options.nudge: New numbers can be fine: the dentist, a new classmate.

options.text: A receipt email for an order you placed this morning
options.nudge: A receipt for something you really bought is normal.

cards.explanation: Real prizes never cost money to claim, and gift cards are a favourite scam payment. A new number or a real receipt can be normal.
cards.hint: What does a real prize cost to claim, and which payment were you told to hang up on?

cards.prompt: A website promises **10,000 free coins** for your favourite game.

steps.text: It asks for your **game username and password** to "send the coins". What do you do?

choices.text: Type them in: lots of comments say it really works
choices.consequence: Scammers write those comments too. The site keeps your password and takes your account. There were never any coins.

choices.text: Close the page: coins only come from the game itself
choices.consequence: Your account stays yours. Free-coin sites are a common trick to steal accounts.

cards.explanation: "Free coins" sites are **too good to be true**. Never type your game password anywhere except the game's own app or website.
cards.hint: Is this too good to be true? And who should ever see your password?

cards.prompt: You have a weekend job at a café. A text arrives from a number you don't know.

steps.text: **"Hi, it's your boss on my new number. Buy three $100 gift cards for a customer and text me the codes. Keep it quiet!"** What do you do?

choices.text: Buy them quickly. Your boss is busy and it sounds urgent
choices.consequence: Gift cards, rushing and secrecy are all scam signs. Once you send the codes, the money is gone.

choices.text: Reply and ask if it's really them
choices.consequence: The reply goes to the scammer, who will happily say yes.

choices.text: Call your boss on the number you already have
choices.consequence: Your boss has no idea what you mean. Scam stopped, and your boss warns the rest of the team.

cards.explanation: Check "new number" texts by contacting the person on the **number you already have**. Gift cards and secrecy are warning signs, whoever it claims to be.
cards.hint: How can you reach your boss in a way a scammer can't fake?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Texts with a **fee**, **deadline** and **link**? Check in the **official app**.
- Calls: **hang up and call back** on a number you know.
- Prizes that cost money to claim are **too good to be true**.

Next: websites that copy the real thing.
